This very simple library, lean-mumi, adds support for mutual blocks with types living in different universes. This also means that it adds support for nested inductives that mix universes. So this works:

import Mumi

mutual
inductive A : Prop where
  | mk : B → A
inductive B : Type where
  | leaf : Nat → B
  | fromA : A → B
end

inductive T : Type where
  | mk1 : T
  | mkT : Nonempty T → T

Either of those declarations would throw an error otherwise. It also reduces in the kernel, and in the compiler, the way you'd want it to:

def bTag : B → Nat :=
  @B.mutualRec (fun _ => True) (fun _ => Nat) (fun _ _ => trivial) (fun n => n) (fun _ _ => 0)

example : bTag (B.leaf 7) = 7 := rfl   -- iota, in the kernel
#eval bTag (B.leaf 7)                  -- 7, in compiled code

It's worth emphasizing that this is done purely as a library you import, without touching Lean's kernel or the type theory. A just-slightly-clever construction lets you derive types with all the correct iota reduction from equal-universe types. This library intercepts the elaborator and, if it fails due to unequal universes, does the lowering to derive these types. Everything goes through the kernel with any unsafe or similar, so it's still just as sound as before and find for proofs.

To make it usable with code in the compiler, a csimp theorem is generated (ultimately relying on Lean's own _unsafe_def recursor compilation). This could have been done with an _unsafe_def auxiliary definition or implemented_by attribute but, in case you don't trust the generated computable definition to match up, this means that the correctness of this code generation is also getting checked as a theorem first.

You should just be able to add this library to your path, import it once, and then these "improved" inductives will hopefully just work! :)

A few examples of what is supported:

-- Mixing different universes
mutual
inductive P3 : Prop where
  | fromQ : Q3 → P3
  | fromR : R3 → P3
inductive Q3 : Type 0 where
  | leaf : Nat → Q3
  | fromP : P3 → Q3
  | wrap : Q3 → Q3
inductive R3 : Type 2 where
  | fromP : P3 → R3
  | higher : Type 1 → R3
  | pair : Q3 → R3 → R3
end

--Mutual nested inductives carrying data
mutual
inductive D5A : Prop where
  | mk : D5B → D5A
inductive D5B : Type where
  | leaf : Nat → D5B
  | node : List D5B → D5B
  | back : D5A → D5B
end

mutual
inductive Total : Prop where
  | mk : Stream' → Total
inductive Stream' : Type 0 where
  | nil : Stream'
  | cons : (Nat → Stream') → Stream'
  | back : Total → Stream'
end

--Indexed types
inductive Ix : Nat → Type where
  | base : Ix 0
  | step : (n : Nat) → Nonempty (Ix n) → Ix (n + 1)

--And yes, the resulting recursors still have the "right" type:
/-- info: Ix.step : (n : Nat) → Nonempty (Ix n) → Ix (n + 1) -/
#guard_msgs in
#check @Ix.step

--Complicated universe variables
mutual
inductive MA : Prop where
  | fromB : MB → MA
  | fromC : MC → MA
inductive MB : Type u where
  | leaf : Nat → MB
  | fromA : MA → MB
inductive MC : Type (max u (max (v + 1) (w + 1))) where
  | fromB : MB → MC
  | big : Type v → Type w → MC
end

Or even all of them together:

mutual
inductive XEv : Nat → Prop where
  | zero : XEv 0
  | succ : (n : Nat) → XOd n → XEv (n + 1)
inductive XOd : Nat → Type u where
  | one : XOd 1
  | succ : (n : Nat) → XEv (n + 1) → XOd n → Nat → XOd (n + 2)
end

/-- info: XOd.{u} : Nat → Type u -/
#guard_msgs in
#check XOd

def xSum : (n : Nat) → XOd.{u} n → Nat :=
  fun n t => @XOd.mutualRec (fun _ _ => True) (fun _ _ => Nat)
    trivial (fun _ _ _ => trivial) 0 (fun _ _ _ k _ ih => ih + k) n t

/-- info: 10 -/
#guard_msgs in
#eval xSum.{0} 5 (.succ 3 (.succ 3 (.succ 1 (.succ 1 .one) .one 4)) (.succ 1 (.succ 1 .one) .one 4) 6)

/-! ## Small elimination at a variable universe

Universes are derived per member, elimination is not: the motives may all land
in `Prop` whatever `u` is. -/

example (b : PB.{u}) : True :=
  @PB.mutualRec (fun _ => True) (fun _ => True) (fun _ => True)
    (fun _ _ => trivial) (fun _ _ => trivial)
    (fun _ => trivial) (fun _ _ => trivial) (fun _ _ => trivial)
    (fun _ _ => trivial) (fun _ => trivial) (fun _ _ _ _ => trivial) b

/-
The constructors are `def`s, so `match` and a bare `cases` do not see them.  The
recursor's minor premises are named after the constructors, so `induction using`
reads the way it would for a real inductive.
-/

example (Γ : Ctx) : 0 ≤ Γ.length := by
  induction Γ using Ctx.recursor with
  | nil => simp [Ctx.length]
  | snoc Γ x h ih => simp

inductive Fam (α : Type) : Nat → Type where
  | mk : α → Fam α n

inductive FamOk (α : Type) : {n : Nat} → Fam α n → Prop where
  | mk {n : Nat} (a : α) : FamOk α (.mk (n := n) a)

inductive OkFam (α : Type) (n : Nat) where
  | mk (v : Fam α n) (h : FamOk α v)

mutual
inductive LocalsII : Type where
  | tip
  | mk : (n : Nat) → (x : OkFam LocalsII n) → LocalsII.Ok n x → LocalsII

It has all the right definitional equalities (iota reduction) in almost all cases, but there's one or two edge cases where it has to fall back to propositional equality, and this is registered as a simp lemma by default. cases, induction, and match blocks all work correctly too.

After some work I've got a decent implementation of induction-recursion! There are two ways to use it, one that uses an extra axiom (corresponding to the existence of Mahlo cardinals in each universe) and gives you the desired universe; the other that puts an induction recursion that "should" be at Type u instead up at Type (u+1) ... but doesn't rely on any axioms.

The tricky part was getting the former to kernel reduce. It's one thing to take an axiom that says "some type exists that's big enough for these-and-these properties", but it's quite another to get a /computable representation/ from that /axiom/. It turned out to require some cleverness with Acc that I'm quite proud of, and I actually have a proof that any such construction must use Acc (or ~equivalent).
